sections.h2: Due dates and payment in halves
sections.html:
The full bill is due on or before December 20 of the levy year. Owners who prefer can pay in two halves: the first by December 20, and the second by June 20 provided the first half was paid in full (Idaho Code 63-903).

Partial payments are accepted whenever you make them. They do not wipe out costs, interest or late charges that already accrued, though. Whatever is left of the first half after December 20 picks up late charges and interest, and the second half does the same after June 20.

A missed or subsequent roll works differently. The tax collector has 30 days after the roll arrives to send the bill, and payment is still due by June 20. After that date the tax is delinquent. A second, unexpected bill on a parcel you are selling is worth a call to the county treasurer to find out if it comes from a missed roll.

sections.h2: The valuation date for your house
sections.html:
Idaho values taxable property as of 12:01 a.m. on January 1 of the year the tax is levied. Real, personal and operating property are all assessed annually at market value as of that moment (Idaho Code 63-205).

Why this matters at sale time: a house that sells in October is still taxed on how it stood the previous January 1. Work done or damage suffered after that date leaves the current bill unchanged. If a house burned or was gutted in the spring and the roll still shows the old condition, take it to the county assessor, and act fast, because appeal windows are strict.

Idaho keeps the assessor, who sets value, separate from the treasurer, who bills and collects. Calls about value go to the first office. Calls about balances, payoff figures and payment history go to the second.

Interest on a delinquency is charged at one percent per month, counted from January 1 following the year the tax lien attached. Interest is not charged on collection costs (Idaho Code 63-1001). Late charges apply on top of interest under section 63-201.

Collected late charges and interest go to the county auditor, who splits them among the taxing districts in proportion to each district's share of the tax. Paying current taxes does not stop a delinquency proceeding already under way for an earlier year (Idaho Code 63-903(7)).

Interest on a balance missed at the December 20 deadline begins the following January 1. The rate is monthly, so a full year of delay means twelve months of it, before late charges and costs. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff figure for the day you plan to close, because the number moves every month.

sections.html:
County offices can add local rules, so confirm dates with your treasurer and assessor.

sections.h2: Programs that lower or delay a home's property tax
sections.html:
The State Tax Commission and county assessors run three homeowner programs. Every one requires its own application, and all sit beside the homestead exemption, which has a separate page.

  • Property Tax Reduction. Savings run from $250 to $1,500, applied to the home plus one acre at most. Qualifying for 2027 means 2026 income after medical expenses of $40,030 or less, plus one of these: age 65 or older, blind, widowed, disabled, a former POW or hostage, or a fatherless or motherless child under 18. File annually from January 1 through April 15. Approval shows as a credit on the December bill.
  • Property Tax Deferral. Taxes on the house and up to an acre are put off, with the tax and interest repaid later. The 2027 income ceiling is $63,400 and the filing window is January 1 to September 7. The state pays the county directly, so your bill shows no deferral.
  • Disabled Veteran benefit. A veteran rated 100% service-connected disabled can see tax cut by as much as $1,500, regardless of income. Filing runs January 1 to April 15 as well.

Fees that local governments charge for solid waste, irrigation and the like are not reduced by any of these programs. A seller who used deferral owes that money back, so check with the assessor on how the balance gets handled before closing.

sections.h2: When an owner stops paying for years
sections.html:
If delinquent real property is not redeemed within three years of the delinquency date, the county tax collector must make a tax deed to the county (Idaho Code 63-1005). The county cannot take the deed until it has given notice of the pending issue and recorded an affidavit of compliance.

The notice rules are specific:

  • Record owners and parties in interest get notice by certified mail with return receipt, sent between five months and two months ahead of the planned deed date.
  • A published notice must run weekly for four straight weeks, and the final run must come at least 14 days before the deed date.
  • Each notice names the owner, describes the parcel, gives the delinquency year, itemizes the amount owed, and states when and where the deed will issue.
  • At least five working days before issuance, the tax collector signs an affidavit of compliance and has it recorded with the county recorder.

Record owners also pay the costs of preparing, serving and publishing the notice, and those costs become a perpetual lien in favor of the tax collector. Even after a tax deed issues, the record owner or a party in interest may still redeem until the county commissioners enter into a contract of sale (Idaho Code 63-1007).

sections.h2: Selling an Idaho house with tax still due
sections.html:
Unpaid property tax does not block a sale. Closing proceeds normally cover the balance. The steps are short, and the order matters.

  1. Request a written payoff from the county treasurer listing each delinquent year, interest and costs, with a good-through date.
  2. Look for any year close to the three-year mark. A parcel nearing a tax deed has a hard deadline that outranks any closing date.
  3. Hand the payoff figure to the title or escrow company so it can be paid out of the proceeds.
  4. Ask the assessor about any homestead exemption, deferral or reduction on the parcel before you transfer.

Timing can trip up a closing. In Kootenai County, escrow may not pay the treasurer when closing falls before annual tax information is available or before the second installment is due, and then the buyer or seller is left holding the credit. Wherever the house is, ask the title company how current-year taxes will be prorated and who actually sends the payment.

Owners with an exemption problem have one more reason to act early. When a house goes to a bona fide purchaser for value before a notice of intent to attach a lien for an improperly claimed exemption is recorded, the assessor and treasurer stop recovering that unpaid amount (Idaho Code 63-602G). The buyer is protected, so clean up any exemption issue before listing.

A cash sale has no lender underwriting or appraisal, so the title work and the payoff set the schedule. Get the tax figure first and the rest tends to follow.

faqs.q: When are Idaho property taxes due?
faqs.a: December 20 for the whole bill. Owners can split it, paying the first half by December 20 and the second by June 20 of the next year, as long as the first half is paid in full.

faqs.q: How much interest does Idaho charge on late property tax?
faqs.a: One percent per month, counted from January 1 following the year the lien attached, plus late charges. Interest is not charged on collection costs.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Idaho house if I owe back property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing proceeds normally pay off the tax, interest and costs. Request a written payoff from the county treasurer and hand it to the title or escrow company.

faqs.q: Does Idaho have help for seniors or disabled homeowners with property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Property Tax Reduction can lower tax by $250 to $1,500 for qualifying owners, the Disabled Veteran benefit can reduce it by up to $1,500, and Property Tax Deferral lets qualifying owners postpone tax, which must be repaid later with interest.

faqs.q: How long before a county can take a house for unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Three years from the delinquency date. If the parcel is still not redeemed, the tax collector must issue a tax deed to the county after proper notice and a recorded affidavit of compliance.
